Based on the retrieved healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that there is a consensus among the experts in the field that even impaired fasting blood glucose (IFG) levels before undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) surgery are associated with an increased risk of mortality. Specifically, studies suggest that patients with IFG and undiagnosed diabetes mellitus (DM) may experience a similar level of increased risk compared to those with type 2 diabetes who have normal fasting glucose levels.

The evidence suggests that patients with IFG or undiagnosed DM are more likely to have severe and adverse clinical outcomes despite achieving glycemic targets. This is because IFG and undiagnosed DM often reflect an underlying condition, such as insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, which may not be apparent on a single blood glucose test.

Furthermore, it's essential to note that patients with IFG or undiagnosed DM who have achieved normal fasting glucose levels at diagnosis may still experience adverse outcomes. This highlights the importance of early case detection and management of these conditions to improve patient outcomes.

The recommended approach is to use an active case detection program to identify patients with IFG or undiagnosed DM, even if they are asymptomatic at diagnosis. Early intervention can help prevent severe and adverse clinical outcomes.

In summary, the consensus among experts suggests that even impaired fasting blood glucose levels preoperatively are associated with increased mortality after CABG surgery, particularly for patients with IFG and undiagnosed DM.
